deep.reconstruction:
Setting (from the preceding pages): X is a topological space and F is a family of subsets of X (eventually the 'tame' sets) satisfying axioms a)–e). These are roughly Boolean stability, closure and interior or local closedness, local finiteness, and (Dim). (Dim) is a descending-chain condition on closed members X1 ⊃ X2 ⊃ … each nowhere dense in the previous one; it is an abstract finiteness of dimension. A cellular decomposition (partition) P of X into locally closed 'leaves' is F-admissible when its leaves lie in F. F_P is then the finite Boolean algebra of unions of leaves. The previous page proves two things by a dimension induction (peel off an open dense part U_i where the family is 'locally constant', then recurse on the nowhere-dense closed complement). First, F is the filtered union of the F_P. Second, admissible decompositions admit finite sups for refinement.

This page, Remarque: assume in addition axiom f). It is presumably a local-connectedness axiom: connected components of members of F are in F and are finite in number, locally. Then there exist F-admissible cellular decompositions with connected leaves (a 'stratification'), such that every Y in a given finite set of members of F is a union of leaves. Among such decompositions there is a coarsest one. The proof is the same as before, except that one replaces each U_i by its connected components. Hence F is the filtered union of the F_P with P having connected leaves, and such decompositions admit finite sups. Heading: 'F-moderate regular cellular decompositions'.

§4 begins an abstract theory of regularity. Grothendieck gives a subfamily F_r ⊂ F of locally closed sets, called the 'F-regular' parts; the model is submanifolds, or sets satisfying some smoothness or equisingularity condition. He imposes axiom (S) (the circled letter): for every closed Y in F, there is a largest relatively open U ⊂ Y belonging to F_r, written Y_reg. Moreover Y_reg is dense in Y, i.e. Y_sing = Y − Y_reg is nowhere dense in Y.

The next page uses this to define F-regular partitions, whose leaves are regular and whose saturated closed sets have saturated singular loci (a frontier-type condition). It proves the existence of a coarsest one by the same induction, now also adding the (U_i)_sing to the list of sets to be respected. It concludes with a canonical F-regular partition of X.

In modern terms, this is an axiomatic, o-minimal-style proof of the existence of a coarsest (canonical) stratification adapted to any regularity condition. The only input is that 'regular points form an open dense set'. This is the Whitney/Mather/Teissier canonical-stratification scheme, formulated for an abstract tame structure.
errors: Gap: the proof that a coarsest decomposition with connected leaves exists is only asserted ('la dém. est la même'). It needs f) to give finitely many (or at least locally finitely many) components, each in F, for every U_i. It also needs the components of U_i to be relatively open, i.e. U_i locally connected in the tame sense. Without this the leaves need not be locally closed or finite in number.

Grothendieck writes that all Y ∈ F are unions of leaves. Literally this cannot hold for all of F; it must mean a given finite subfamily, as in the earlier Cor. 1 / F_P setting. This is a slip of formulation.

Condition (S) asks for density of Y_reg in every closed Y ∈ F. This is a strong genericity axiom. For Whitney-type conditions, regularity is a property of pairs of strata rather than of single sets, so this formulation of §4 covers 'smooth locus' type regularity directly. Frontier or pair conditions only enter through the saturation requirement on the next page.

ideas.what: Abstract family F of 'tame' subsets with finiteness and dimension axioms; F as filtered union of finite Boolean algebras F_P attached to admissible cell decompositions
ideas.modern_name: o-minimal structures / cell decomposition theorem; tame topology
ideas.usually_credited_to: van den Dries (1984), Pillay–Steinhorn (1986), Knight–Pillay–Steinhorn; precursors Łojasiewicz, Hironaka, Hardt (semialgebraic/subanalytic)
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme (1984), §5–6, programmatically only, without these axioms or proofs

ideas.what: Connected-leaf version: F-admissible stratifications with connected strata, coarsest one, finite sups for refinement
ideas.modern_name: existence of finite stratifications with connected strata compatible with finitely many definable sets
ideas.usually_credited_to: standard in o-minimal geometry (van den Dries, Tame Topology and o-minimal structures, 1998)

ideas.what: Abstract regularity class F_r with axiom: the maximal regular open subset Y_reg of any closed tame Y exists and is dense; leading to a coarsest/canonical F-regular stratification
ideas.modern_name: canonical (minimal) stratification with respect to a generic stratifying condition
ideas.usually_credited_to: Whitney (1965), Mather, Teissier (1982, canonical Whitney stratification), Loi (o-minimal Whitney stratifications, 1998); axiomatic treatments of 'stratifying conditions' later (e.g. Nguyen–Trivedi–Trotman, Halupczok and coauthors)
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme mentions canonical stratifications/dévissages in tame topology in general terms

missed.claim: In 1974, a decade before o-minimality, Grothendieck sets up an axiomatic framework (a family F with axioms a)–f) and a regular subfamily F_r with a 'regular locus is open dense' axiom). From it he derives, by a uniform dimension-induction, (i) coarsest compatible stratifications with connected strata and (ii) a canonical coarsest F-regular stratification, for any abstract regularity notion. The general principle 'any generic stratifying condition yields a canonical stratification in a tame category' was later established piecemeal: Teissier for analytic Whitney; Loi and others for o-minimal; axiomatic versions only recently.
missed.quote: Pour Y∈F, Y fermé, parmi les parties rel. ouvertes U de Y qui sont ∈ F_r, il y en a une plus grande, Y_reg, et celle-ci est dense dans Y
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It documents Grothendieck's priority on an axiomatic canonical-stratification theorem inside a tame framework. The details are absent from Esquisse, which is only programmatic. This is of historical interest for o-minimal geometry and stratification theory; it is mathematically not new today.

deep.surprise_reason: It is known in general that Grothendieck anticipated tame topology, from Esquisse. Here, however, the 1974 notes already contain a concrete axiomatic cell-decomposition and canonical-regular-stratification argument. The mathematics itself is now standard in o-minimal geometry, so this is a notable unpublished historical detail rather than a new result.
transcription_corrections: The circled axiom label read as '(B)' is most likely '(S)': the next page refers to 'la condition (S) sur F_r'.
Line 4: 'stratifiée [?] des P' is better read as an uncertain word before 'des P (i.e. à feuilles connexes)'. The crossed-out item after a)b)c) is '(Dims)'/(Dim), replaced by 'd) e)'.
'que parmi les P, il y en a une plus grossière' is correct; the following words read 'La dém. est la même'.
In §4, 'formée d'éléments de F loc. fermés' is correct (inserted 'loc.').
